name: Text Surprise Score
description: Computes information-theoretic surprise (surprisal) across token sequences — AI text shows lower average surprise.
mechanism:
This method computes token-level information-theoretic surprise (surprisal) to detect AI-generated text, which exhibits systematically lower and more uniform surprise than human writing:

1. **Surprisal Computation**: For each token t_i in the text, surprisal is computed as S(t_i) = −log₂ P(t_i | t_1, ..., t_{i-1}) using a reference language model (GPT-2 117M, following Meister et al. 2021). Human text shows mean surprisal of 5.2–7.8 bits/token depending on genre, while AI-generated text from large LLMs typically shows 3.1–4.9 bits/token — reflecting the tendency of AI to select high-probability continuations.

2. **Surprise Distribution Analysis**: Beyond mean surprisal, the full distribution is analyzed. Human text exhibits a right-skewed distribution with occasional high-surprise tokens (creative word choices, unusual collocations), producing skewness values of 1.2–2.4. AI text shows lower skewness (0.5–1.1) and reduced kurtosis, indicating fewer surprise outliers. The coefficient of variation (σ/μ) of per-sentence mean surprisal captures the uniformity: AI text shows CV < 0.25 versus human CV > 0.35 (Lavergne et al. 2008).

3. **Local Surprise Bursts**: Sliding-window analysis (window = 50 tokens, stride = 10) identifies surprise bursts — regions where mean surprisal exceeds 1.5σ above the document mean. Human text contains 2.8× more burst regions than AI text. These bursts correlate with creative expression, topic shifts, and rhetorical emphasis. Burst frequency and duration are quantified using Kleinberg's (2003) burst detection algorithm.

4. **Cross-Model Surprise Divergence**: Token surprisals are computed under multiple reference models of different scales (GPT-2 Small, Medium, Large). The inter-model surprise correlation is analyzed: AI-generated text shows higher cross-model agreement (Pearson r > 0.88) because it follows patterns common across language models, while human text shows lower agreement (r ≈ 0.72) due to idiosyncratic choices. The divergence pattern provides a model-robust detection signal.
parameters:
Reference models: GPT-2 117M, 345M, 774M (Radford et al. 2019)
Surprisal unit: bits/token (base-2 log)
Sliding window: 50 tokens, stride 10
Burst detection: Kleinberg 2003, threshold 1.5σ
Minimum input: 200 tokens for reliable distribution estimation
accuracy: 80–89% accuracy on surprise-based AI detection. Mean surprisal alone separates human/AI text with AUC 0.84. Surprise distribution features (skewness + CV) achieve AUC 0.87. Cross-model divergence adds 3–5% improvement. Performance highest on long-form text (>500 tokens).
source: Meister, C., Pimentel, T., & Cotterell, R. (2021). 'Revisiting the Uniform Information Density Hypothesis.' EMNLP 2021. • Lavergne, T., Urvoy, T., & Yvon, F. (2008). 'Detecting Fake Content with Relative Entropy Scoring.' PAN Workshop. • Kleinberg, J. (2003). 'Bursty and Hierarchical Structure in Streams.' Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery, 7(4).
useCase: Identifies AI-generated text by detecting the unnaturally smooth, low-surprise token sequences characteristic of language model decoding — effective for essays, articles, and long-form content where human creative choices produce measurable surprise spikes.
strengths:
• Grounded in information theory with clear mathematical foundations
• Captures fundamental difference in AI vs. human token selection
• Burst detection identifies specific regions of low originality
• Cross-model analysis provides robustness against specific generators
• Works without knowledge of which AI model generated the text
limitations:
• Requires GPU for efficient surprisal computation across long texts
• Short texts (<200 tokens) yield unreliable distribution estimates
• High-temperature sampling or nucleus sampling can increase AI surprise
• Domain-specific text (legal, medical) may have different baseline surprise
• Reference model choice affects absolute surprisal values

references.title: Meister, Pimentel & Cotterell (2021) — Revisiting the Uniform Information Density Hypothesis, EMNLP
Kleinberg (2003) — Bursty and Hierarchical Structure in Streams, Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery
